newsitem.title: UK: Dollar ends Europe day where it began, eyes Rubin.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends Europe day where it began, eyes Rubin.

text.p: The dollar finished European trading near where it began, with players reluctant to stick their necks out before a 1730 GMT speech by U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin ahead of his visit to Japan on Friday.
The spectre of Japan's huge trade surplus with the U.S. haunts the market at present, and fears Rubin could dilute his strong dollar stance will cap dollar/yen for now, traders said.
"The risk-reward is probably more in favour of being short dollar/yen rather than long going into the (Tokyo) meeting," said Ian Amstad, international economist at Bankers Trust in London.

"If the meeting is conspicuously unproductive and does nothing to resolve trade tensions with the Japanese surplus on the rise, the forex markets might conclude the reaction is to take dollar/yen lower," he added.

Rubin will talk with Japan's prime minister and finance minister when he visits Tokyo en route to an APEC meeting in the Philippines at the weekend. He was due to address New York Stock Exchange directors, among others, at 1730 GMT on Wednesday.
The dollar was quoted at 122.68/73 yen at 1541 GMT compared to 122.58/68 in early Europe and 122.69/74 in late dealings here on Tuesday.
The U.S. unit rallied smartly from a session low of 121.95, helped by relief that the Bank of Japan's quarterly "Tankan" survey was not as upbeat as some in the market had feared.

The key index of major manufacturers' mood improved to plus two from minus three last time -- its first positive reading since 1991 -- but dealers said it revealed insecurity about the future and left little scope for tightening monetary policy.

"It was very middle-of-the-road -- the theory is (Japanese) interest rates aren't going to change any time soon," said Peter Wood, forex trader at Bank of Boston. Talk of a strong Tankan sparked hefty yen buying overnight before its release, he added.

Dollar/yen also fell overnight when Rubin made clear a renewed rise in the Japanese trade surplus was not in the U.S. interest. Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's assertion that he wanted the yen to be a strong currency did not help.
Dollar/mark had an aimless session, trading at 1.6717/22 at 1602 GMT versus an opening 1.6710/15 and late Tuesday's 1.6705/10.
The market shrugged off February factory orders data, which came in a fraction below consensus forecasts with a 0.8 percent rise, well down from January's 2.5 percent increase.
It kept a weather eye, however, on Wall Street.
The Dow Jones, which unsettled the U.S. currency with its big losses on Monday and last Thursday, was trading down nearly 51 points, or 0.77 percent, at 6561.20 by 1624 GMT.
"We look as if we're marking time here and taking our cue from the stock market," said Bank of Boston's Wood.

The market is on the alert for a follow-up to last week's Fed rate hike, but traders and analysts said the dollar's current fixation with U.S. stocks means it is unlikely to enjoy the textbook rally if rates go up again.
The markets' next major clue on U.S. rates is due on Friday, when March non-farm payrolls data will appear, analysts said.
Economists are rooting for an average 182,000 increase in payrolls, down from the 339,000 rise in February, with unemployment seen ticking down to 5.2 percent from 5.3.
The closely-watched average hourly earnings component of the employment report, however, is predicted to rise to 0.4 percent from 0.2.
-- Abigail Levene, London Newsroom +44-171-542-8968
